reader.title: Whipping of Monroe Lyon
bases: Unknown parties took Monroe Lyon out at night and severely whipped him as a 'penalty' for his part in a quarrel, and five men were arrested for the whipping (A2, A3).

Two separately sourced reports, the Oxford Ledger as quoted by the Durham Recorder and the Durham Globe as quoted by the News and Observer, agree that Lyon was severely whipped after the beating of Mrs. Hall (A2, A3).

summary.text: The whipping of Monroe Lyon was a night attack on a Black man at Green's Station, a village on the O. & C. Railroad, apparently in North Carolina, in late July 1890, in which unknown parties took him out and severely whipped him.
The whipping followed a quarrel in which Lyon's wife was accused of beating a neighbor, Mrs. John L. Hall, and Lyon of holding back the Halls' daughter.
Five men were later arrested for the whipping, and Lyon's wife and children left the neighborhood.
According to the Oxford Ledger, the Lyons' daughter had repeatedly passed through Mrs. Hall's yard despite warnings, and on a Saturday Mrs. Hall tried to eject her.
The Ledger said that Mrs. Lyon then appeared with a stick and beat Mrs. Hall, while Monroe Lyon seized and held the Hall daughter as she ran to help her mother.
After Mrs. Lyon struck Mrs. Hall again with a tobacco stick on Sunday, "the negroes" were all arrested, to be tried before 'Squire J. D. Tilley on Saturday.
That night, by the Ledger's account, Monroe Lyon "was taken out" by "unknown parties and severely whipped."
A visitor from Green's Station told the Durham Globe that Lyon was disabled by the whipping, although none of his bones were broken.
His wife and children had left the neighborhood, and five men had been arrested for the whipping; no outcome of their postponed hearing was reported.
The story reached print on August 6, 1890, through two local papers, the Oxford Ledger and the Durham Globe, as quoted by the Durham Recorder and the Raleigh News and Observer.

The Durham Recorder ran the Oxford Ledger account under the headline "Brutal Attack Upon a Lady," praising Mrs. Hall as "one of the good ladies" of the village and calling the Lyons a "miserable gang of negroes."
That account treated the whipping as justified, saying Lyon "has suffered the penalty" for holding Miss Hall.
The Raleigh News and Observer, quoting the Durham Globe under "Sensation at Green's Station," gave no judgment and reported the arrest of five men for the whipping.
Neither paper named the whippers or gave their race, and no Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

accounts.label: Oxford Ledger (via Durham Recorder)
accounts.gist: Mrs. Lyon beat Mrs. Hall in her yard on Saturday while Monroe Lyon held the Hall daughter, attacked her again Sunday with a tobacco stick, and that night unknown parties took Lyon out and severely whipped him as 'the penalty.'

accounts.label: Durham Globe (via News and Observer)
accounts.gist: A visitor from Green's Station said excitement had not subsided; Lyon was disabled by the whipping, his wife and children had left, and five men had been arrested for the whipping, with the hearing postponed.

framing.detail: The Durham Recorder's 'Brutal Attack Upon a Lady' (from the Oxford Ledger) praised Mrs. Hall as 'one of the good ladies,' called the Lyons a 'miserable gang of negroes,' and said Lyon 'has suffered the penalty' by being whipped.
The News and Observer's 'Sensation at Green's Station' (from the Durham Globe) reported Lyon's injuries and the arrest of five men for the whipping without comment.

versions.value: five men arrested for whipping him

conflicts.note: Not a contradiction: the later Durham Globe report records arrests made after the Oxford Ledger account.
